Adding 1 to \( (n + 1)! \) gives us \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), which is a number that is at least \( 2 \) greater than \( (n + 1)! \), confirming that \( (n + 1)! + 1 \geq 2 \).

Given that \( p \) divides both \( (n + 1)! \) and \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), it must also divide their difference:

By the definition of factorial, \(N\) is greater than 1, and all the primes in our list are factors of \((n + 1)!\). Therefore, if \(N\) had any of these primes as factors, it would have to divide both \((n + 1)!\) and \(N = (n + 1)! + 1\), which is impossible because their difference is 1:

\[ N - (n + 1)! = 1 \]

Any number that divides both \(N\) and \((n + 1)!\) must also divide 1. But 1 is not a prime number, which contradicts the fact that all prime numbers divide \(N\). Therefore, our assumption that only finitely many primes exist must be false, proving that there are infinitely many primes.
